questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: In the gynoecium of a flower, NCERT describes structures that arise from the placenta and are the megasporangia. These megasporangia are commonly called:

options.text: Ovules
Ovaries
Embryo sacs
Locules

solution.explanation: NCERT: inside the ovary is the ovarian cavity (locule); the placenta is located inside it, and arising from the placenta are the megasporangia, commonly called ovules. The embryo sac (female gametophyte) lies inside the nucellus of the ovule, so it is not the sporangium itself.
solution.why_others_wrong: The ovary encloses the ovules, the locule is the ovarian cavity, and the embryo sac is the female gametophyte formed inside the ovule.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants', pre-fertilisation: the pistil, megasporangium (ovule) and embryo sac
solution.final_answer: Option A: Ovules

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: In transverse section, a typical angiosperm anther is a four-sided (tetragonal) structure. Where are its microsporangia located?

options.text: All four in the centre, around the connective
One at each corner of a single lobe, the other lobe being sterile
At the four corners, two in each lobe
Two at the corners and two along the middle of the anther

solution.concept: Arrangement of microsporangia in an anther
solution.explanation: NCERT: the anther is a four-sided (tetragonal) structure consisting of four microsporangia located at the corners, two in each lobe. This fits the bilobed, dithecous anther: each lobe has two theca, and each theca contains one microsporangium.
steps: At the corners, two in each lobe
solution.why_others_wrong: NCERT places the microsporangia at the corners, not in the centre, and both lobes are fertile, with two microsporangia each.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants', pre-fertilisation: stamen, microsporangium and pollen grain
solution.final_answer: Option C: At the four corners, two in each lobe

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: The nucleus of the functional megaspore divides mitotically to form two nuclei. According to NCERT, these two nuclei:

options.text: Fuse with each other to form a diploid nucleus
Move to the opposite poles, forming the 2-nucleate embryo sac
Move to the opposite poles, and a cell wall is laid down between them at once
Both remain at the micropylar end and directly form the egg apparatus

solution.concept: Early development of the embryo sac
solution.explanation: NCERT: the nucleus of the functional megaspore divides mitotically to form two nuclei, which move to the opposite poles, forming the 2-nucleate embryo sac. Two more sequential mitotic nuclear divisions give the 4-nucleate and then the 8-nucleate stages. These divisions are strictly free nuclear: cell walls are laid down only after the 8-nucleate stage.
steps: 2-nucleate embryo sac; walls come only after the 8-nucleate stage
solution.why_others_wrong: The nuclei do not fuse; no wall forms at this stage because the divisions are free nuclear; and the egg apparatus is organised only after the 8-nucleate stage.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants', pre-fertilisation: female gametophyte
solution.final_answer: Option B: Move to the opposite poles, forming the 2-nucleate embryo sac

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: Plants such as Viola, Oxalis and Commelina bear cleistogamous flowers, which do not open at all. How does pollination take place in these flowers?

options.text: Insects carry pollen to them from the chasmogamous flowers of the same plant
Wind carries pollen from other plants through small openings in the petals
Pollen grains are carried by water to the stigma after the bud is submerged
The anthers dehisce in the flower buds, and the pollen grains come in contact with the stigma

solution.explanation: NCERT: in cleistogamous flowers the anthers and stigma lie close to each other. When the anthers dehisce in the flower buds, the pollen grains come in contact with the stigma to effect pollination. Such flowers are invariably autogamous, since there is no chance of cross-pollen landing on the stigma.
steps: Anthers and stigma lie close together
Anthers dehisce inside the bud → autogamy
solution.why_others_wrong: A closed flower cannot receive pollen from insects, wind or water; that is why cleistogamous flowers are invariably autogamous.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants', pollination: kinds of pollination (autogamy)
solution.final_answer: Option D: The anthers dehisce in the flower buds, and the pollen grains come in contact with the stigma

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: As the ovules mature into seeds, the ovary develops into a fruit; the transformation of ovules into seeds and of the ovary into a fruit proceeds simultaneously.
Statement II: Most fruits develop only from the ovary and are called true fruits.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Seed and fruit formation; true fruits
solution.explanation: NCERT: as ovules mature into seeds, the ovary develops into a fruit, i.e. the transformation of ovules into seeds and ovary into fruit proceeds simultaneously (Statement I true). In a few species such as apple, strawberry and cashew, the thalamus also contributes to the fruit (false fruits); most fruits, however, develop only from the ovary and are called true fruits (Statement II true).
steps: Statement II: true (true fruits from the ovary only)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants', post-fertilisation: seed and fruit
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): It is believed that the distribution of some bryophytes and pteridophytes is limited.
Reason (R): In these plants, water is needed for the transport of the male gametes and for fertilisation.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Water and the male gametes of lower plants
solution.explanation: NCERT contrasts the rarity of water pollination in flowering plants with lower plant groups (algae, bryophytes and pteridophytes), in which water is a regular mode of transport for the male gametes. It states that, particularly for some bryophytes and pteridophytes, their distribution is believed to be limited because of the need for water for the transport of male gametes and fertilisation. R is the very reason given for A.
steps: R: true (water carries the male gametes)
R is the stated cause of A
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants', pollination: agents of pollination (water)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: NCERT describes two ways in which apomictic seeds may develop. Which of them does it say happens more often?

options.text: A diploid egg cell is formed without reduction division and develops into the embryo without fertilisation
The primary endosperm cell develops into an embryo instead of an endosperm
Some nucellar cells surrounding the embryo sac start dividing, protrude into the embryo sac and develop into embryos, as in many Citrus and mango varieties
A synergid is fertilised by the second male gamete and develops into an extra embryo

solution.explanation: NCERT: there are several ways of development of apomictic seeds. In some species, the diploid egg cell is formed without reduction division and develops into the embryo without fertilisation. More often, as in many Citrus and mango varieties, some of the nucellar cells surrounding the embryo sac start dividing, protrude into the embryo sac and develop into embryos; in such species each ovule contains many embryos.
steps: Way 1 ('in some species'): unreduced diploid egg → embryo
solution.why_others_wrong: The unreduced-egg route is described for 'some species', not as the commoner route; NCERT gives no apomixis from the primary endosperm cell or from a fertilised synergid.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants', apomixis and polyembryony
solution.final_answer: Option C: Some nucellar cells surrounding the embryo sac start dividing, protrude into the embryo sac and develop into embryos, as in many Citrus and mango varieties

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Following compatible pollination, the contents of the pollen grain move into the pollen tube, which grows through the tissues of the stigma and style and reaches the ovary.
Statement II: The pollen tube can emerge from any point on the pollen grain, because sporopollenin forms a continuous layer over the whole exine.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Germination of the pollen grain on the stigma
solution.explanation: NCERT: following compatible pollination, the pollen grain germinates on the stigma to produce a pollen tube through one of the germ pores; the contents of the pollen grain move into the pollen tube, which grows through the tissues of the stigma and style and reaches the ovary (Statement I true). The exine has prominent apertures, the germ pores, where sporopollenin is absent; the tube emerges through one of them, not from any point (Statement II false).
steps: Tube emerges through a germ pore → Statement II false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants', pollination: pollen-pistil interaction
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Compare microsporogenesis and megasporogenesis in a typical flowering plant. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) In both, a diploid spore mother cell divides by meiosis to give four haploid spores.
(b) All four microspores of a tetrad normally develop into pollen grains, whereas in a majority of flowering plants only one of the four megaspores is functional.
(c) Both the male and the female gametophyte develop from a haploid spore by mitotic division.
(d) The pollen mother cell is differentiated in the micropylar region of the nucellus.
(e) The four megaspores dissociate from each other as the anther dehydrates.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: (a), (b), (c) and (d) only
(a), (b) and (c) only
(b), (c) and (e) only
(a), (d) and (e) only

solution.concept: Spore formation and gametophyte development compared
solution.explanation: (a) True: a pollen mother cell gives a microspore tetrad by meiosis, and the megaspore mother cell gives four megaspores by meiosis. (b) True: as the anthers mature, the microspores dissociate and develop into pollen grains, while in most flowering plants one megaspore is functional and three degenerate. (c) True: the microspore nucleus divides mitotically to form the vegetative and generative cells, and the functional megaspore nucleus divides mitotically to form the embryo sac. (d) False: it is the megaspore mother cell that is differentiated in the micropylar region of the nucellus. (e) False: it is the microspores that dissociate as the anther dehydrates.
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (d) or (e) include a male feature given to the female side or the reverse; '(b), (c) and (e)' also leaves out the true statement (a).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants', pre-fertilisation: microsporogenesis, megasporogenesis and the female gametophyte
solution.final_answer: Option B: (a), (b) and (c) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: In an artificial hybridisation experiment with a female parent bearing bisexual flowers, a worker removes the anthers only after they have dehisced. Why is this a mistake, according to the logic of NCERT's procedure?

options.text: Anthers that have dehisced can no longer be removed with forceps
Dehisced anthers secrete chemicals that make the stigma permanently non-receptive
Emasculation is never needed in bisexual flowers, so the worker should not have removed the anthers
Pollen of the same flower may already have reached the stigma, so some seeds may come from self-pollination instead of the desired cross

solution.concept: Purpose of emasculation before anther dehiscence
solution.explanation: NCERT: in crossing experiments it is important that only the desired pollen grains are used and the stigma is protected from contamination. If the female parent bears bisexual flowers, the anthers are removed from the flower bud before the anther dehisces (emasculation), and the flower is then bagged. Once the anthers have dehisced, the flower's own pollen may already have contaminated the stigma, defeating the purpose.
steps: Goal: only the desired pollen on the stigma
Remove them in the bud, before dehiscence
solution.why_others_wrong: The problem is contamination, not difficulty of removal or a chemical effect; and emasculation is exactly what NCERT requires for bisexual flowers.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants', pollination: artificial hybridisation
solution.final_answer: Option D: Pollen of the same flower may already have reached the stigma, so some seeds may come from self-pollination instead of the desired cross

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Wind-pollinated flowers often have a large, often feathery stigma.
Reason (R): A large, feathery stigma can easily trap air-borne pollen grains.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: wind-pollinated flowers often have well-exposed stamens (so that pollen is easily dispersed into wind currents) and a large, often feathery stigma to easily trap air-borne pollen grains. Since wind carries pollen at random, a large trapping surface raises the chance that pollen lands on the stigma. R gives the function for which the feature in A exists.
steps: R: true, the purpose of the feathery stigma
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants', pollination: agents of pollination (wind)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Consider where reserve food is found in mature seeds of the plants named in NCERT. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) In a mature pea seed, the endosperm has been consumed, and the food reserves lie in the thick, swollen cotyledons.
(b) In a mature castor seed, a part of the endosperm persists and is used up during seed germination.
(c) In a mature beet seed, a persistent remnant of the nucellus is present.
(d) In coconut, the endosperm is completely consumed by the embryo before the seed matures.
(e) In groundnut, the endosperm persists in the mature seed.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: (a), (b), (c) and (d) only
(a), (b) and (c) only
(b), (d) and (e) only
(a), (c) and (e) only

solution.explanation: NCERT: the endosperm may be completely consumed by the developing embryo before seed maturation (pea, groundnut, beans), or it may persist in the mature seed (castor and coconut) and be used up during seed germination. In legumes the cotyledons are thick and swollen due to storage of food reserves. In black pepper and beet, remnants of the nucellus persist as the perisperm. So (a), (b) and (c) are true; (d) and (e) reverse the cases of coconut and groundnut.
steps: Pea, groundnut: endosperm consumed; cotyledons store food
solution.why_others_wrong: Coconut keeps its endosperm and groundnut does not, so options with (d) or (e) are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants', post-fertilisation: endosperm; seed
solution.final_answer: Option B: (a), (b) and (c) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The megaspore mother cell is differentiated in the micropylar region of the nucellus, and the embryo later develops at the micropylar end of the embryo sac, where the zygote is situated.
Statement II: In a mature embryo sac, the three antipodal cells lie at the micropylar end, next to the egg apparatus.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Polarity of the ovule and embryo sac
solution.explanation: NCERT: ovules generally differentiate a single megaspore mother cell in the micropylar region of the nucellus, and the embryo develops at the micropylar end of the embryo sac where the zygote is situated (Statement I true). In the mature embryo sac, three cells are grouped together at the micropylar end (the egg apparatus) and three cells, the antipodals, are at the chalazal end (Statement II false).
steps: MMC: micropylar region; embryo: micropylar end → I true
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants', pre-fertilisation: female gametophyte; post-fertilisation: embryo
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (event) with List-II (where it takes place).

List-I:
A. Meiosis of the megaspore mother cell
B. Meiosis of the pollen mother cell
C. Syngamy and triple fusion
D. Germination of a compatible pollen grain

List-II:
I. Stigma
II. Embryo sac
III. Nucellus of the ovule
IV. Microsporangium of the anther

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I
A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II
A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I
A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I

solution.concept: Sites of the main reproductive events
solution.explanation: The megaspore mother cell lies in the micropylar region of the nucellus and divides there by meiosis (A-III). Pollen mother cells develop from the sporogenous tissue of the microsporangium and undergo meiosis there (B-IV). The pollen tube releases the two male gametes into a synergid of the embryo sac, where one fuses with the egg (syngamy) and the other with the polar nuclei in the central cell (triple fusion) (C-II). A compatible pollen grain germinates on the stigma (D-I).
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap the two meiotic sites, put fertilisation on the stigma, or put megaspore formation in the embryo sac, which forms only after meiosis.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants', pre-fertilisation events; double fertilisation
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about apomixis and polyembryony are correct according to NCERT?

(a) When seeds of orange are squeezed, many embryos of different sizes and shapes can be seen from each seed.
(b) In species in which nucellar cells develop into embryos, each ovule contains many embryos.
(c) Scientists are working to understand the genetics of apomixis and to transfer apomictic genes into hybrid varieties.
(d) Polyembryony means the presence of more than one embryo sac in an ovule.
(e) Apomixis is found in all members of Asteraceae and grasses.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: (a), (b), (c) and (d) only
(a), (b) and (e) only
(c), (d) and (e) only
(a), (b) and (c) only

solution.concept: Polyembryony and the hope of apomictic hybrids
solution.explanation: NCERT: in many Citrus and mango varieties, nucellar cells protrude into the embryo sac and develop into embryos, so each ovule contains many embryos (b); squeezing orange seeds shows many embryos of different sizes and shapes from each seed (a). Many scientists are working to understand the genetics of apomixis and to transfer apomictic genes into hybrid varieties (c). Polyembryony is the occurrence of more than one embryo in a seed, not of extra embryo sacs (d false), and apomixis is seen in some species of Asteraceae and grasses, not all (e false).
solution.why_others_wrong: Any option with (d) or (e) contains a false statement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants', apomixis and polyembryony
solution.final_answer: Option D: (a), (b) and (c) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: A plant of genotype Aa is self-pollinated. Megasporogenesis is normal and monosporic, and each seed forms by normal double fertilisation. In what fraction of the seeds will the embryo be Aa and the endosperm AAa?

solution.concept: Genotypes of embryo and endosperm in the same seed
solution.explanation: All nuclei of an embryo sac come by mitosis from one haploid megaspore, so the egg and both polar nuclei carry the same allele (A or a, probability 1/2 each). Both male gametes of a pollen grain come from one generative cell, so they carry the same allele (A or a, 1/2 each). Embryo Aa with endosperm AAa needs a female gametophyte carrying A (endosperm gets A + A from the polar nuclei) and a pollen grain carrying a: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. (The other Aa embryos, from an a embryo sac and an A pollen grain, have endosperm Aaa.)
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/2 counts every Aa embryo, including those with endosperm Aaa; 1/16 wrongly treats the egg and each polar nucleus as receiving alleles independently; 3/4 is the fraction of embryos carrying at least one A.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants', pre-fertilisation: female gametophyte; double fertilisation
solution.final_answer: Option B: 1/4

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
In a plant of genotype Aa, seeds are formed after cross-pollination with pollen from a plant of genotype aa. Which of the following are expected to be genetically identical to the mother plant (Aa) in every seed or fruit?

(a) The seed coat
(b) The perisperm, in a species that has one
(c) The pericarp
(d) A nucellar embryo, in a species with nucellar polyembryony
(e) The endosperm

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: (a), (b) and (c) only
(a), (c), (d) and (e) only
(a), (b), (c) and (d) only
(b), (d) and (e) only

solution.concept: Maternal tissues in seeds and fruits
solution.explanation: The seed coat develops from the integuments, the perisperm is the persistent nucellus, and the pericarp develops from the ovary wall: all three are tissues of the mother sporophyte, so they are Aa. A nucellar embryo arises from a diploid nucellar cell without fertilisation, so it is also Aa. The endosperm develops from the triple-fused primary endosperm cell: here it is AAa or aaa, never identical to the mother.
steps: Nucellar embryo: maternal; endosperm: AAa or aaa
solution.why_others_wrong: '(a), (b) and (c) only' leaves out the nucellar embryo; options with (e) include the triploid endosperm, which carries the paternal allele.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants', post-fertilisation: seed and fruit; apomixis and polyembryony
solution.final_answer: Option C: (a), (b), (c) and (d) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: A species with bisexual flowers shows self-incompatibility. A bee carries pollen from one flower to the stigma of another flower on the same plant. What is the expected outcome?

options.text: Fertilisation occurs, because the pollen came from a different flower and so counts as cross-pollen
The pistil recognises the pollen as 'self' and inhibits pollen germination or pollen tube growth, so the ovules are not fertilised by it
The pollen tube grows normally, but the endosperm fails to form
Fertilisation occurs, because self-incompatibility acts only against autogamy within a flower

solution.explanation: Transfer of pollen to another flower of the same plant is geitonogamy, which is genetically similar to autogamy since the pollen comes from the same plant. Self-incompatibility is a genetic mechanism that prevents self-pollen (from the same flower or other flowers of the same plant) from fertilising the ovules by inhibiting pollen germination or pollen tube growth in the pistil. The pistil's recognition of the pollen, followed by acceptance or rejection, is the result of a dialogue between pollen and pistil.
steps: Germination or tube growth inhibited → no fertilisation
solution.why_others_wrong: Geitonogamous pollen is genetically self-pollen, so it is rejected at germination or tube growth; NCERT does not describe rejection at the endosperm stage.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants', outbreeding devices; pollen-pistil interaction
solution.final_answer: Option B: The pistil recognises the pollen as 'self' and inhibits pollen germination or pollen tube growth, so the ovules are not fertilised by it

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): An ovule generally has a single embryo sac.
Reason (R): Ovules generally differentiate a single megaspore mother cell, and in a majority of flowering plants only one of the four megaspores it forms is functional and develops into the embryo sac.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Why one embryo sac per ovule
solution.explanation: NCERT: an ovule generally has a single embryo sac formed from a megaspore. Ovules generally differentiate a single megaspore mother cell; its meiosis gives four megaspores, and in a majority of flowering plants one is functional while the other three degenerate. Only the functional megaspore develops into the female gametophyte. One mother cell × one functional megaspore = one embryo sac, so R explains A.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants', pre-fertilisation: megasporogenesis and the female gametophyte
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
A flowering plant has 2n = 24 and sheds its pollen at the 3-celled stage.

Given below are two statements:

Statement I: At the time of shedding, one pollen grain contains 36 chromosomes in all, counting all its nuclei.
Statement II: Before fertilisation, the central cell of a mature embryo sac of this plant contains 36 chromosomes.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: n = 12. A pollen grain shed at the 3-celled stage has one vegetative cell and two male gametes, i.e. three haploid nuclei: 3 × 12 = 36 (Statement I true). The central cell of the embryo sac has two haploid polar nuclei: 2 × 12 = 24 chromosomes before fertilisation. It becomes triploid (36) only after triple fusion (Statement II false).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants', pre-fertilisation: pollen grain and female gametophyte
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
A plant species has small flowers that are not colourful and produce no nectar. The pollen grains are light, non-sticky and produced in very large numbers, the stigma is large and feathery, each ovary has a single ovule, and many flowers are packed into an inflorescence. Which inferences are reasonable on the basis of NCERT?

(a) The species is most probably wind-pollinated.
(b) The pollen grains reaching a given stigma is a chance factor, which is why so much pollen is produced.
(c) The species could well be a grass, in which this mode of pollination is quite common.
(d) Nectar-robbing insects are probably its main pollinators.
(e) Its pollen grains are probably protected from wetting by a mucilaginous covering.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: (a), (b), (c) and (e) only
(a), (d) and (e) only
(b), (c) and (d) only
(a), (b) and (c) only

solution.explanation: All the features listed match NCERT's description of wind-pollinated flowers: light, non-sticky pollen; a large, often feathery stigma; a single ovule in each ovary and numerous flowers packed into an inflorescence; flowers not very colourful and without nectar (a). Since contact of pollen with the stigma is a chance factor in wind pollination, the flowers produce an enormous amount of pollen compared with the number of ovules (b). NCERT notes that wind pollination is quite common in grasses (c). (a) Segregation of the two alleles of a gene can be explained by the separation of the pair of homologous chromosomes carrying them during gamete formation.
(b) Independent assortment of two genes can be explained by the independent segregation of two different pairs of chromosomes carrying them.
(c) Two genes that are very tightly linked on the same chromosome do not assort independently, and parental combinations predominate among the progeny.
(d) A gamete receives both chromosomes of each homologous pair.
(e) The law of independent assortment applies to every pair of genes, whatever their location.

(b), (c) and (d) only
(a), (d) and (e) only
(a), (b) and (c) only

In NCERT's comparison of chromosomes and genes, independent pairs segregate independently of each other, which explains independent assortment (b). Morgan found that genes on the same chromosome, especially tightly linked ones, give mostly parental combinations, so they do not assort independently (c). Only one chromosome of each pair goes to a gamete (d false), and linkage shows that independent assortment does not apply to every gene pair (e false).
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (d) or (e) include a false statement; '(b), (c) and (d)' also leaves out (a).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', chromosomal theory of inheritance; linkage and recombination

(e) Her father must be colour blind.

(a), (b) and (c) only
(a), (b) and (e) only
(c), (d) and (e) only

She has two X chromosomes, one from each parent, so the allele could have come from either a carrier mother or a colour-blind father (c), and her father need not be colour blind (e false). Each daughter receives one of her two X chromosomes, so a daughter is not necessarily a carrier (d false).

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: A couple with normal colour vision has a son with Klinefelter's syndrome (XXY) who is red-green colour blind. Assuming no new mutation, which explanation fits these facts?

options.text: A sperm carrying both the X and the Y chromosome of the father fertilised a normal egg carrying the colour-blindness allele
The mother is a carrier, and an egg carrying two X chromosomes, both with the colour-blindness allele, was fertilised by a Y-bearing sperm
An egg with no sex chromosome was fertilised by a sperm carrying both the X and the Y chromosome of the father
The father is a carrier of colour blindness and passed the allele to his son on the Y chromosome

Both X chromosomes must therefore come from the mother, who must be a carrier (she sees normally); her egg had two X chromosomes (failure of segregation, aneuploidy) and was fertilised by a Y-bearing sperm.
steps: Son needs the allele on both X chromosomes
Father's X is normal → neither X came from him
Both X from a carrier mother + Y from father
solution.why_others_wrong: Any option in which the son receives his father's X gives him a normal allele; a male cannot be a carrier, and the gene is not on the Y chromosome.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', sex-linked inheritance; chromosomal disorders
solution.final_answer: Option B: The mother is a carrier, and an egg carrying two X chromosomes, both with the colour-blindness allele, was fertilised by a Y-bearing sperm

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Each dihybrid in List-I is test-crossed with aabb.

Match List-I (dihybrid test-crossed with aabb) with List-II (expected fraction of aabb progeny).

List-I:
A. AaBb, with the two genes on different chromosomes
B. A dihybrid that received AB from one parent and ab from the other, with 20 per cent recombination
C. A dihybrid that received Ab from one parent and aB from the other, with 20 per cent recombination
D. A dihybrid that received AB from one parent and ab from the other, with genes so tightly linked that no recombination occurs

List-II:
I. 1/2
II. 1/4
III. 1/10
IV. 2/5

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I
A-I, B-IV, C-III, D-II
A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I
A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III

solution.concept: Test-cross outcomes with and without linkage
solution.explanation: In a test cross, the fraction of aabb progeny equals the fraction of ab gametes of the dihybrid. Independent genes: 1/4 (A-II). AB/ab with 20 per cent recombination: ab is parental, (1 − 0.2)/2 = 0.4 = 2/5 (B-IV). Ab/aB with 20 per cent recombination: ab is recombinant, 0.2/2 = 0.1 = 1/10 (C-III). Complete linkage of AB/ab: only AB and ab gametes, 1/2 (D-I).
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes confuse the coupling (AB/ab) and repulsion (Ab/aB) arrangements, or treat complete linkage as independent assortment.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
In a bird species, the somatic cells of both sexes have 78 chromosomes. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The hen produces two kinds of eggs, each with 39 chromosomes: one kind carries a Z chromosome and the other a W chromosome.
(b) The cock produces only one kind of sperm with respect to the sex chromosomes.
(c) The sex of a chick is decided by the kind of egg that is fertilised.
(d) The somatic cells of the hen have 77 chromosomes, because she has only one Z chromosome.
(e) Each sperm of the cock carries 38 autosomes and a W chromosome.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: (a), (b), (c) and (d) only
(b), (c) and (e) only
(a), (b) and (c) only
(a), (d) and (e) only

solution.explanation: In birds the female is ZW and the male ZZ, so both sexes have the same number of chromosomes, 76 autosomes + 2 sex chromosomes = 78 (d false). The hen gives eggs with 38 autosomes + Z or 38 autosomes + W, 39 each (a). The cock gives only sperms with 38 autosomes + Z (b); it has no W (e false). Since the egg type varies and the sperm does not, the egg decides the sex of the chick (c).
steps: Hen ZW, cock ZZ: 78 in both
Sperms: 38 + Z only → egg decides sex
solution.why_others_wrong: (d) treats the ZW female like an XO male; (e) gives the male a W chromosome, which only females carry.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: The scheme of DNA replication in which each strand of the double helix acts as a template for the synthesis of a new complementary strand was proposed by:

options.text: Watson and Crick themselves
Meselson and Stahl
Taylor and colleagues
Hershey and Chase

solution.concept: Proposal and proof of semiconservative replication
solution.explanation: NCERT: while proposing the double helix structure, Watson and Crick also proposed a scheme for replication: the two strands separate and each acts as a template for a new complementary strand, so that each daughter molecule has one parental and one new strand (semiconservative). Meselson and Stahl (1958) later proved it experimentally in E. coli, and Taylor and colleagues showed it for chromosomes of Vicia faba.
steps: Proved in E. coli: Meselson and Stahl
solution.why_others_wrong: Meselson and Stahl and Taylor provided experimental proof; Hershey and Chase showed that DNA is the genetic material.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', replication: the experimental proof
solution.final_answer: Option A: Watson and Crick themselves

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: According to NCERT, a nucleotide has three components. They are:

options.text: A nitrogenous base, a hexose sugar and a phosphate group
A nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar and an amino acid
Two nitrogenous bases joined by hydrogen bonds and a phosphate group
A nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar and a phosphate group

solution.explanation: NCERT: a nucleotide has three components: a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar (ribose in RNA, deoxyribose in DNA) and a phosphate group. A base linked to the sugar is a nucleoside; adding a phosphate at the 5'-OH gives a nucleotide.
solution.why_others_wrong: The sugar is a pentose, not a hexose; amino acids are not part of nucleotides; hydrogen-bonded base pairs belong to the double helix, not to a single nucleotide.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', structure of polynucleotide chain
solution.final_answer: Option D: A nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar and a phosphate group

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The base sequence of an mRNA is the same as that of the coding strand of its gene, except that the mRNA has uracil in place of thymine.
Reason (R): The mRNA is synthesised complementary to the template strand, and the template strand is itself complementary to the coding strand.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Why mRNA matches the coding strand
solution.explanation: NCERT: in a transcription unit, the strand with 3'→5' polarity acts as the template, and the other strand, with 5'→3' polarity, has the same sequence as the RNA (except thymine at the place of uracil) and is called the coding strand. The RNA is built by complementary base pairing on the template; since the coding strand is also complementary to the template, the RNA and the coding strand carry the same sequence, with U in RNA where DNA has T. R is the direct cause of A.
steps: So RNA = coding strand (U for T)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', transcription: transcription unit
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: RNA, being a catalyst as well as genetic material, was reactive and hence unstable.
Statement II: DNA has evolved from RNA with chemical modifications that make it more stable.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: From the RNA world to DNA
solution.explanation: NCERT (RNA world): RNA was the first genetic material and used to act both as genetic material and as a catalyst. But RNA, being a catalyst, was reactive and hence unstable (Statement I true). Therefore DNA has evolved from RNA with chemical modifications that make it more stable; being double stranded, with a complementary strand, DNA further resists changes by evolving a process of repair (Statement II true).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', RNA world
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (enzyme or catalyst) with List-II (role).

List-I:
A. DNA-dependent DNA polymerase
B. DNA ligase
C. DNA-dependent RNA polymerase
D. 23S rRNA in bacteria (ribozyme)

List-II:
I. Joins the discontinuously synthesised fragments
II. Forms peptide bonds during translation
III. Synthesises RNA on a DNA template

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

A-IV, B-II, C-III, D-I
A-IV, B-I, C-III, D-II
A-I, B-IV, C-III, D-II

solution.concept: Enzymes of replication, transcription and translation
solution.explanation: DNA-dependent DNA polymerases polymerise deoxyribonucleotides using a DNA template (A-IV). The discontinuously synthesised fragments of the lagging strand are later joined by DNA ligase (B-I). Transcription is catalysed by DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (C-III). In bacteria, 23S rRNA acts as the enzyme (ribozyme) for peptide bond formation (D-II).

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: The pentose sugar present in the nucleotides of DNA is:

options.text: Ribose
2'-deoxyribose
Glucose
3'-deoxyribose

solution.explanation: NCERT: the pentose sugar is ribose in RNA and 2'-deoxyribose in DNA, which is why the nucleic acids are named ribonucleic acid and deoxyribonucleic acid. RNA retains a 2'-OH group on every nucleotide, which makes it labile; DNA lacks it.
solution.why_others_wrong: Ribose is the sugar of RNA, glucose is a hexose, and the missing oxygen in DNA's sugar is at the 2' carbon, not the 3' carbon.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', structure of polynucleotide chain
solution.final_answer: Option B: 2'-deoxyribose

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Which of the following nitrogenous bases are pyrimidines?

(a) Cytosine
(b) Thymine
(c) Uracil
(d) Adenine
(e) Guanine

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: (a), (d) and (e) only
(d) and (e) only
(a), (b) and (d) only
(a), (b) and (c) only

solution.explanation: NCERT: nitrogenous bases are of two types, purines (adenine and guanine) and pyrimidines (cytosine, uracil and thymine). Cytosine is common to DNA and RNA; thymine is present in DNA and uracil in RNA.
solution.why_others_wrong: Adenine and guanine are purines, so options with (d) or (e) are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', structure of polynucleotide chain
solution.final_answer: Option D: (a), (b) and (c) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: A mutant E. coli has an altered operator to which the lac repressor can no longer bind; its i, z, y and a genes and its promoter are normal. Glucose is absent. What happens in this mutant?

options.text: The z, y and a genes are never transcribed, even when lactose is present
The z, y and a genes are transcribed only when lactose is present, as in the wild type
The z, y and a genes are transcribed even when lactose is absent
Only the i gene is transcribed, and the repressor accumulates in the cell

solution.concept: Role of the operator in negative regulation
solution.explanation: In the lac operon, the repressor (from the i gene) binds to the operator and prevents RNA polymerase from transcribing the structural genes; the inducer acts by inactivating the repressor. If the repressor cannot bind the operator, nothing blocks RNA polymerase, so the polycistronic z-y-a mRNA is made whether or not lactose is present: the operon is expressed all the time.
steps: Repressor must bind operator to switch the operon off
Operator cannot bind repressor → never switched off
z, y, a transcribed even without lactose
solution.why_others_wrong: Nothing stops transcription in this mutant, so it cannot be 'never' or 'only with lactose'; the i gene is transcribed in the wild type too and its product simply cannot act here.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', regulation of gene expression: the lac operon
solution.final_answer: Option C: The z, y and a genes are transcribed even when lactose is absent

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When the lac operon is switched on, the z, y and a genes are transcribed together.
Reason (R): In the lac operon, a polycistronic structural gene is regulated by a common promoter and regulatory genes.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Polycistronic organisation of the lac operon
solution.explanation: NCERT: in bacteria, the arrangement in which a polycistronic structural gene is regulated by a common promoter and regulatory genes is called an operon. The lac operon's structural genes z, y and a share one promoter and operator, so when the repressor is removed by the inducer, RNA polymerase transcribes them as one polycistronic mRNA. R explains A.
steps: One promoter for z, y, a
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', regulation of gene expression: the lac operon
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Because the bases pair in a complementary way, if the sequence of bases in one strand of a DNA double helix is known, the sequence in the other strand can be predicted.
Statement II: A circular double-stranded DNA molecule of 5386 base pairs has 10,772 phosphodiester linkages in all.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: base pairing confers a very unique property on the polynucleotide chains: they are complementary, so if the sequence of one strand is known, the other can be predicted (Statement I true). In a circular strand of n nucleotides there are n phosphodiester linkages (a linear strand has n − 1). Two strands of 5386 nucleotides each: 2 × 5386 = 10,772 (Statement II true).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', structure of polynucleotide chain
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subtopic: Human genome project and DNA fingerprinting
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the significance and findings of the Human Genome Project are correct according to NCERT?

(a) Knowledge about the effects of DNA variations among individuals can lead to revolutionising the ways to diagnose, treat and someday prevent thousands of disorders that affect human beings.
(b) Learning about non-human organisms' DNA sequences can lead to an understanding of their natural capabilities that can be applied to challenges in health care, agriculture, energy production and environmental remediation.
(c) Since less than 2 per cent of the genome codes for proteins, the remaining DNA has been shown to have no role at all.
(d) The human genome contains about 80,000 genes.
(e) The functions of all the discovered human genes are now known.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: (a), (b) and (d) only
(b), (c) and (e) only
(a), (c) and (d) only
(a) and (b) only

solution.concept: Why the Human Genome Project matters
solution.explanation: NCERT: knowledge about the effects of DNA variations among individuals can revolutionise the ways to diagnose, treat and someday prevent thousands of disorders (a); learning about the DNA of non-human organisms can lead to an understanding of their natural capabilities, applicable to health care, agriculture, energy production and environmental remediation (b). Repetitive sequences, though thought to have no direct coding function, shed light on chromosome structure, dynamics and evolution (c false). The genome has about 30,000 genes, not 80,000 (d false), and functions are unknown for over 50 per cent of the discovered genes (e false).

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (experiment) with List-II (label used).

List-I:
A. Hershey and Chase: labelling the DNA of bacteriophages
B. Hershey and Chase: labelling the protein coat of bacteriophages
C. Meselson and Stahl: replication in E. coli
D. Taylor and colleagues: replication in chromosomes of Vicia faba

List-II:
I. Radioactive thymidine
II. ¹⁵NH₄Cl as the only nitrogen source
III. Radioactive sulphur
IV. Radioactive phosphorus

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I
A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I
A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II
A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I

solution.explanation: DNA contains phosphorus but not sulphur, and protein contains sulphur but not phosphorus, so Hershey and Chase labelled phage DNA with radioactive phosphorus (A-IV) and the protein coat with radioactive sulphur (B-III). Meselson and Stahl grew E. coli on ¹⁵NH₄Cl as the only nitrogen source to make heavy DNA (C-II). Taylor and colleagues used radioactive thymidine on Vicia faba to detect the distribution of newly synthesised DNA in chromosomes (D-I).
steps: P in DNA, S in protein
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap the two Hershey–Chase labels or the two replication experiments.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', the search for genetic material; replication: the experimental proof

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: In a variation of Griffith's experiment, mice are injected with a mixture of heat-killed S strain and heat-killed R strain Streptococcus pneumoniae. What is expected?

options.text: The mice die, because the R strain is transformed by the S strain
The mice die, because heat-killed S strain bacteria alone are virulent
The mice live, because no living bacteria are present to be transformed or to multiply
The mice live, but living S strain bacteria are recovered from them

solution.explanation: NCERT (Griffith): live S strain kills mice; live R strain and heat-killed S strain alone do not. Only when heat-killed S was mixed with live R did the mice die, because the living R bacteria were transformed into virulent S bacteria. With both strains heat-killed, there are no living cells to be transformed or to cause infection, so the mice survive and no living bacteria can be recovered.
solution.why_others_wrong: Dead R cells cannot be transformed; heat-killed S alone is not virulent; and no living S cells can be recovered without living bacteria.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', the search for genetic material: transforming principle
solution.final_answer: Option C: The mice live, because no living bacteria are present to be transformed or to multiply

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
The template strand of a short stretch of a structural gene reads 3'-TACGAT-5'. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The mRNA transcribed from it reads 5'-AUGCUA-3'.
(b) The coding strand reads 5'-ATGCTA-3'.
(c) The first codon of the mRNA is the initiation codon AUG.
(d) The mRNA contains thymine at two positions.
(e) The RNA is polymerised in the 3'→5' direction.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: (a), (b), (c) and (d) only
(a), (b) and (c) only
(b), (c) and (e) only
(a), (d) and (e) only

solution.explanation: RNA is complementary and antiparallel to the template: template 3'-TACGAT-5' gives mRNA 5'-AUGCUA-3' (a). The coding strand has the same sequence as the mRNA with T for U: 5'-ATGCTA-3' (b). The first codon AUG is the initiation codon (c). RNA has uracil, not thymine (d false), and all nucleic acid polymerases add nucleotides in the 5'→3' direction (e false).

solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (d) or (e) contain a false statement; '(b), (c) and (e)' also omits (a).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', transcription: transcription unit

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In eukaryotes, RNA polymerase I transcribes the rRNAs 28S, 18S and 5.8S, whereas RNA polymerase III transcribes the 5S rRNA.
Statement II: In eukaryotes, the heterogeneous nuclear RNA, the precursor of mRNA, is transcribed by RNA polymerase III.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Division of labour among eukaryotic RNA polymerases
solution.explanation: NCERT: in eukaryotes there are at least three RNA polymerases in the nucleus. RNA polymerase I transcribes rRNAs (28S, 18S and 5.8S); RNA polymerase III transcribes tRNA, 5S rRNA and snRNAs (Statement I true); RNA polymerase II transcribes the precursor of mRNA, hnRNA (Statement II false).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', transcription: transcription unit and gene
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In bacteria, the mRNA does not require any processing to become active.
Reason (R): Bacterial structural genes are split genes, with coding sequences interrupted by introns.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: in bacteria the mRNA does not require any processing to become active, and since transcription and translation occur in the same compartment, translation can begin before the mRNA is fully transcribed (A true). Split genes, with exons interrupted by introns, are a feature of eukaryotes; their hnRNA must be spliced. Bacterial genes are not split, so R is false.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', transcription: transcription unit and gene; processing of hnRNA

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: One strand of a double-stranded DNA molecule has the base composition A 30 per cent, T 20 per cent, G 15 per cent and C 35 per cent. What percentage of all the bases in the double-stranded molecule is guanine?

options.text: 15 per cent
35 per cent
50 per cent
25 per cent

solution.concept: Base composition of a double helix from one strand
solution.explanation: Each G in one strand pairs with a C in the other. The complementary strand therefore has G = 35 per cent (opposite the C of the first strand). Total G = (15 + 35)/2 = 25 per cent of the bases of the double helix. Check with Chargaff's rule: then C = 25, and A = T = (30 + 20)/2 = 25 per cent each.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15 per cent is the G of one strand only; 35 per cent is the G of the other strand only; 50 per cent is G + C, not G alone.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', structure of polynucleotide chain: double helix and Chargaff's rule
solution.final_answer: Option D: 25 per cent

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (E. coli strain (glucose absent)) with List-II (behaviour of the lac operon).

List-I:
A. Wild type
B. Mutant whose operator cannot bind the repressor
C. Mutant whose repressor binds the operator but cannot interact with the inducer
D. Mutant lacking the lac promoter

List-II:
I. Expressed only when lactose is present
II. Expressed even when lactose is absent
III. Not expressed even when lactose is present, because the repressor stays bound
IV. Not expressed, because RNA polymerase has no binding site

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: A-I, B-III, C-II, D-IV
A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV
A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV
A-I, B-II, C-IV, D-III

solution.concept: Predicting lac operon behaviour in mutants
solution.explanation: Wild type: the repressor blocks the operator; lactose (inducer) inactivates it, so the operon is inducible (A-I). If the operator cannot bind the repressor, nothing blocks RNA polymerase and the genes are expressed even without lactose (B-II). If the repressor cannot interact with the inducer, it stays bound to the operator even when lactose is present (C-III). The promoter provides the binding site for RNA polymerase; without it, transcription cannot start (D-IV).

solution.final_answer: Option B: A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
The coding strand of a short gene reads 5'-ATGGCATTCTAA-3'. Use: AUG = methionine, GCA = alanine, UUC = phenylalanine, UUU = phenylalanine, UAA = stop.

Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The mRNA reads 5'-AUGGCAUUCUAA-3'.
(b) The polypeptide formed is methionine–alanine–phenylalanine.
(c) Deleting the fifth base of the gene would leave the amino acid sequence unchanged.
(d) Changing the ninth base of the coding strand from C to T would not change the polypeptide.
(e) The template strand, written 5'→3', reads 5'-ATGGCATTCTAA-3'.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: (a), (b) and (d) only
(a), (b), (c) and (d) only
(a), (d) and (e) only
(b), (c) and (e) only

solution.concept: Codons, mutations and the degenerate code
solution.explanation: mRNA = coding strand with U for T: AUG GCA UUC UAA (a): Met–Ala–Phe, then stop (b). Deleting the fifth base (C) gives AUG GAU UCU AA…: the reading frame shifts and the amino acids after the first change (c false). C→T at the ninth base turns UUC into UUU, which also codes for phenylalanine, since the code is degenerate (d). The sequence in (e) is the coding strand; the template, written 5'→3', is 5'-TTAGAATGCCAT-3' (e false).

solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', genetic code; mutations and genetic code; translation
solution.final_answer: Option A: (a), (b) and (d) only

questions.subtopic: Human genome project and DNA fingerprinting
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): DNA fingerprinting uses repetitive (satellite) DNA rather than the protein-coding sequences.
Reason (R): Satellite DNA sequences show a high degree of polymorphism among individuals.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Why satellite DNA is used in fingerprinting
solution.explanation: NCERT: DNA fingerprinting involves identifying differences in some specific regions of the DNA sequence called repetitive DNA. Satellite DNA sequences normally do not code for any proteins, but they form a large portion of the human genome and show a high degree of polymorphism, which forms the basis of DNA fingerprinting. Since 99.9 per cent of the bases are the same in all people, it is the highly polymorphic regions that can tell individuals apart: R explains A.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
One DNA molecule of E. coli fully labelled with ¹⁵N (both strands heavy) replicates semiconservatively for several generations in a medium containing only ¹⁴NH₄Cl.

Statement I: After any number of generations (one or more), exactly two of the descendant molecules are hybrid (¹⁵N/¹⁴N), and all the others are light.
Statement II: Heavy (¹⁵N/¹⁵N) DNA reappears after the third generation in the ¹⁴N medium.

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Fate of parental strands in semiconservative replication
solution.explanation: In semiconservative replication the two parental heavy strands are never broken or lost; in each generation each one is paired with a new light strand. So after every generation exactly two molecules are hybrid and the rest are ¹⁴N/¹⁴N (Statement I true): e.g. 2 of 4 after two generations, 2 of 8 after three. A heavy/heavy molecule needs two ¹⁵N strands together, which cannot form in a medium supplying only ¹⁴N (Statement II false).
steps: Two parental strands persist, each in a hybrid
Hybrid count stays 2; light molecules increase
No new ¹⁵N strands → no heavy DNA
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', replication: the experimental proof
