questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: When certain exotic species are introduced into a geographical area, they may become invasive and spread fast, because the invaded land does not have their natural predators.
Statement II: Predators always drive their prey species to extinction.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: one reason why certain exotic species become invasive and spread fast when introduced into a geographical area is that the invaded land does not have their natural predators, as with the prickly pear cactus in Australia (Statement I true). Predators in nature are 'prudent': a predator that overexploits its prey might itself become extinct for lack of food, and predators keep prey populations under control rather than eliminating them (Statement II false).
steps: Prudent predators; prey kept under control → Statement II false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Organisms and Populations', populations: population interactions (predation)
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about plant defences against herbivores are correct?

(a) Thorns, as in Acacia and cactus, are the most common morphological means of defence.
(b) Many plants produce and store chemicals that make the herbivore sick when eaten, inhibit feeding or digestion, disrupt its reproduction or even kill it.
(c) Nicotine, caffeine, quinine, strychnine and opium are produced by plants as defences against grazers and browsers.
(d) Plants produce these chemicals mainly to attract herbivores.
(e) Calotropis is heavily browsed by cattle and goats.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: (a), (b) and (c) only
(a), (b), (c) and (e) only
(b), (c) and (d) only
(a), (d) and (e) only

solution.concept: Morphological and chemical defences of plants
solution.explanation: NCERT: since plants cannot run away, they have evolved morphological and chemical defences. Thorns (Acacia, cactus) are the most common morphological means of defence (a). Many plants produce and store chemicals that make the herbivore sick, inhibit feeding or digestion, disrupt reproduction or kill it (b); nicotine, caffeine, quinine, strychnine and opium are such defences (c). These chemicals deter rather than attract herbivores (d false), and Calotropis produces highly poisonous cardiac glycosides, so cattle and goats never browse on it (e false).
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (d) or (e) contain a false statement; '(b), (c) and (d)' also omits (a).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Organisms and Populations', populations: population interactions (predation)
solution.final_answer: Option A: (a), (b) and (c) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
For a population with r = 0.2 per year, compare the exponential model dN/dt = rN with the logistic model dN/dt = rN[(K − N)/K], taking K = 1000.

Match List-I (model and population size) with List-II (growth rate (individuals per year)).

List-I:
A. Exponential, N = 400
B. Logistic, N = 400
C. Logistic, N = 900
D. Logistic, N = 1000

List-II:
I. 0
II. 18
III. 48
IV. 80

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I
A-IV, B-II, C-III, D-I
A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II
A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I

solution.concept: Exponential and logistic growth rates compared
solution.explanation: Exponential: 0.2 × 400 = 80 (A-IV). Logistic at 400: 0.2 × 400 × 600/1000 = 48 (B-III). Logistic at 900: 0.2 × 900 × 100/1000 = 18 (C-II). At N = K = 1000: 0.2 × 1000 × 0 = 0; the population has reached its asymptote (D-I).
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap the exponential and logistic values at N = 400, or the logistic values at 900 and 1000.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Organisms and Populations', populations: population growth
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
The age structure of three populations is: P: pre-reproductive 45 per cent, reproductive 40 per cent, post-reproductive 15 per cent; Q: 35, 36 and 29 per cent; R: 15, 45 and 40 per cent.

Which of the following inferences are correct?

(a) The age pyramid of P has a broad base and indicates an expanding population.
(b) The age pyramid of R is urn-shaped and indicates a declining population.
(c) The age pyramid of Q is bell-shaped and indicates a stable population.
(d) Population P is declining, since its post-reproductive group is the smallest.
(e) Population R has the broadest base of the three pyramids.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: (a), (b), (c) and (d) only
(b), (c) and (e) only
(a), (b) and (c) only
(a), (d) and (e) only

solution.explanation: The shape of the age pyramid reflects the growth status of a population. P has more pre-reproductive than reproductive individuals: broad base, expanding (a). R has far fewer pre-reproductive than reproductive individuals: narrow base, urn-shaped, declining (b). In Q the pre-reproductive and reproductive groups are nearly equal: bell-shaped, stable (c). A small post-reproductive group does not make P decline (d false), and R has the narrowest, not the broadest, base (e false).
solution.why_others_wrong: (d) judges growth from the post-reproductive group; (e) reverses the base widths.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Organisms and Populations', populations: population attributes (age pyramids)
solution.final_answer: Option C: (a), (b) and (c) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: Two populations of the same species grow exponentially with the same r = 0.02 per year: one starts with 100 individuals and the other with 10,000. Which statement about the time each takes to double is correct? (Nₜ = N₀e^(rt); ln 2 = 0.693)

options.text: The smaller population doubles 100 times faster
The larger population doubles 100 times faster
The doubling times cannot be compared without knowing the carrying capacity
Both take the same time, about 35 years, because the doubling time depends only on r

solution.explanation: Doubling means Nₜ = 2N₀: 2N₀ = N₀e^(rt), so e^(rt) = 2 and t = ln 2/r = 0.693/0.02 ≈ 34.7 years. N₀ cancels: under exponential growth, every population with the same r doubles in the same time, whatever its starting size, although the larger population adds far more individuals in that time.
solution.why_others_wrong: Starting size does not affect the doubling time in the exponential model, and K does not appear in it.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Organisms and Populations', populations: population growth (exponential growth)
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both take the same time, about 35 years, because the doubling time depends only on r

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Write the effect of an interaction on each partner as + (benefit), − (harm) or 0 (no effect).

Which of the following pairings are correct?

(a) Fig and its pollinating wasp: (+, +)
(b) Cattle egret and grazing cattle: (+, 0)
(c) Orchid growing as an epiphyte and the mango branch it grows on: (+, 0)
(d) Cuscuta and the hedge plant on which it grows: (+, 0)
(e) Clown fish and the sea anemone among whose tentacles it lives: (+, +)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: (a), (b) and (c) only
(a), (b), (c) and (e) only
(b), (c) and (d) only
(a), (d) and (e) only

solution.explanation: Fig and wasp: the wasp pollinates the fig while using its fruit for egg laying and larval food; both benefit, mutualism (a). Cattle egrets catch insects stirred up by cattle, which are not affected: commensalism (b). The epiphytic orchid benefits while the mango tree gets no benefit or harm: commensalism (c). Cuscuta is a parasite deriving nutrition from the host, so the host is harmed: (+, −) (d false). The clown fish gets protection, and the sea anemone does not appear to derive any benefit: (+, 0), not (+, +) (e false).
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (d) or (e) mislabel parasitism or commensalism; '(b), (c) and (d)' also omits (a).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Organisms and Populations', populations: population interactions
solution.final_answer: Option A: (a), (b) and (c) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
NCERT lists the important components of the functional aspects of an ecosystem, with a pond as its example. Which of the following are among them?

(a) Productivity
(b) Decomposition
(c) Energy flow
(d) Stratification
(e) Species composition

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: (a), (b), (c) and (d) only
(a), (b) and (c) only
(c), (d) and (e) only
(a), (d) and (e) only

solution.concept: Structural and functional aspects of an ecosystem
solution.explanation: NCERT: the important components of an ecosystem's function are (i) productivity, (ii) decomposition, (iii) energy flow and (iv) nutrient cycling. Species composition (identification and enumeration of species) and stratification (vertical distribution of species at different levels) are features of an ecosystem's structure.
steps: Functions: productivity, decomposition, energy flow, nutrient cycling
solution.why_others_wrong: Stratification and species composition describe structure, not function, so options with (d) or (e) are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Ecosystem', ecosystem: structure and function
solution.final_answer: Option B: (a), (b) and (c) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: According to NCERT, the autotrophic components of a pond ecosystem include:

options.text: Zooplankton and the free-swimming and bottom-dwelling animals
Phytoplankton, some algae, and the floating, submerged and marginal plants found at the edges
Fungi, bacteria and flagellates at the bottom of the pond
Only the rooted plants at the edges; phytoplankton are consumers

solution.explanation: NCERT describes the pond: the abiotic component is the water with dissolved inorganic and organic substances and the rich soil deposit at the bottom; the autotrophic components include the phytoplankton, some algae and the floating, submerged and marginal plants found at the edges; the consumers are zooplankton and the free-swimming and bottom-dwelling forms; and the decomposers are fungi, bacteria and flagellates, especially abundant at the bottom.
steps: Autotrophs: phytoplankton, algae, floating, submerged and marginal plants
solution.why_others_wrong: Zooplankton and animals are consumers; fungi, bacteria and flagellates are decomposers; phytoplankton are producers.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Ecosystem', ecosystem: structure and function (pond)
solution.final_answer: Option B: Phytoplankton, some algae, and the floating, submerged and marginal plants found at the edges

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: NCERT's ideal pyramid of energy shows that primary producers convert only about 1 per cent of the energy in the sunlight available to them into net primary productivity.
Statement II: In an energy pyramid, the energy at a lower trophic level is always more than at a higher level.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT's figure of an ideal pyramid of energy notes that primary producers convert only 1 per cent of the energy in the sunlight available to them into NPP (Statement I true). The pyramid of energy is always upright: energy at a lower trophic level is always more than at a higher level, because some energy is lost as heat at each step (Statement II true).
steps: Statement I: true (1 per cent into NPP)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Ecosystem', ecological pyramids
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Decomposers are heterotrophic organisms.
Reason (R): Decomposers make their own food by photosynthesis.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: decomposers are heterotrophic organisms, mainly fungi and bacteria, which meet their energy and nutrient requirements by degrading dead organic matter (detritus); they are also called saprotrophs. A is true. They do not photosynthesise, so R is false.
steps: Energy from dead organic matter, not photosynthesis → R false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Ecosystem', energy flow: detritus food chain
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: The gross primary productivity of a grassland averages 4 g m⁻² day⁻¹ (dry weight), and the plants use 25 per cent of it in respiration. Taking a year as 365 days, what is the net primary productivity of the grassland in g m⁻² yr⁻¹?

solution.concept: Net primary productivity and its units
solution.explanation: NPP = GPP − R = 4 − (0.25 × 4) = 3 g m⁻² day⁻¹. NCERT expresses productivity per unit area per year, so 3 × 365 = 1,095 g m⁻² yr⁻¹.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1,460 is the annual GPP (respiration not subtracted); 365 is the annual respiration loss; 3 is the daily NPP, not the yearly value.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Ecosystem', productivity
solution.final_answer: Option B: 1,095

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: In cold, waterlogged bogs, partly decomposed plant remains accumulate over many years. Which explanation fits NCERT's account of decomposition?

options.text: Water-soluble nutrients are leached away, so decomposers have nothing to act on
Cold, wet conditions speed up humification and mineralisation
Detritivores multiply rapidly in waterlogged soil and convert all detritus into humus at once
Low temperature and anaerobiosis inhibit decomposition, resulting in a build-up of organic materials

solution.explanation: NCERT: decomposition is largely an oxygen-requiring process, and its rate is controlled by the chemical composition of the detritus and by climatic factors. Warm and moist environments favour decomposition, whereas low temperature and anaerobiosis inhibit it, resulting in the build-up of organic materials. A cold, waterlogged bog combines both inhibiting conditions.
steps: Decomposition inhibited → organic matter builds up
solution.why_others_wrong: Leaching removes only soluble nutrients, not the detritus; cold, wet, anoxic conditions slow, not speed, decomposition; and detritivores do not thrive under anaerobiosis.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Ecosystem', decomposition
solution.final_answer: Option D: Low temperature and anaerobiosis inhibit decomposition, resulting in a build-up of organic materials

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
In a lake, phytoplankton are eaten by zooplankton and by molluscs; small fish eat zooplankton; large fish eat small fish and molluscs; and kingfishers eat small fish and large fish. Take producers as the first trophic level.

Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The molluscs are herbivores (primary consumers).
(b) The large fish occupies the third and the fourth trophic levels.
(c) The kingfisher occupies the fourth and the fifth trophic levels.
(d) The small fish is a primary consumer.
(e) The zooplankton are producers.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: (a), (b), (c) and (d) only
(a), (b) and (c) only
(b), (c) and (e) only
(a), (d) and (e) only

solution.concept: Trophic levels in a food web
solution.explanation: Phytoplankton (1) → molluscs and zooplankton (2): both are primary consumers; NCERT names molluscs as the common herbivores of aquatic ecosystems (a). Small fish eat zooplankton: level 3, a secondary consumer (d false). Large fish eat molluscs (level 3) and small fish (level 4) (b). Kingfishers eat small fish (level 4) and large fish (levels 4 and 5) (c). Zooplankton are consumers (e false).
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (d) or (e) contain a false statement; '(b), (c) and (e)' also omits (a).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Ecosystem', energy flow: food chains and food web
solution.final_answer: Option B: (a), (b) and (c) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Identical leaf litter can decompose at different rates in two regions, because decomposition is controlled by climatic factors such as temperature and soil moisture.
Statement II: Humus is decomposed rapidly by microbes, so it cannot serve as a reservoir of nutrients.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: the rate of decomposition is controlled by the chemical composition of the detritus and by climatic factors; temperature and soil moisture are the most important climatic factors (Statement I true). Humus is highly resistant to microbial action and undergoes decomposition at an extremely slow rate; being colloidal, it serves as a reservoir of nutrients (Statement II false).
steps: Humus: extremely slow decomposition, nutrient reservoir → Statement II false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Ecosystem', decomposition
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: In a grassland, the counts per unit area are: primary producers 58,42,000; primary consumers 7,08,000; secondary consumers 3,54,000; tertiary consumers 3. About how many primary consumers are there for each tertiary consumer, and what is the shape of this pyramid of numbers?

options.text: About 2; upright
About 2.4 lakh; upright
About 2.4 lakh; inverted
About 19 lakh; inverted

solution.explanation: Primary consumers per tertiary consumer = 7,08,000/3 = 2,36,000 ≈ 2.4 lakh. The numbers fall at each higher trophic level (58,42,000 > 7,08,000 > 3,54,000 > 3), with producers forming the broad base and top carnivores the apex, so the pyramid is upright.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 is the ratio of primary to secondary consumers; the pyramid is not inverted, since every level has fewer individuals than the one below; 19 lakh divides the producers by 3.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Ecosystem', ecological pyramids
solution.final_answer: Option B: About 2.4 lakh; upright

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
In a grazing food chain, the producers fix 50,000 kJ. The herbivores obtain 10 per cent of the producers' energy, the primary carnivores 15 per cent of the herbivores' energy, and the secondary carnivores 20 per cent of the primary carnivores' energy.

Match List-I (quantity) with List-II (energy (kJ)).

List-I:
A. Energy obtained by the herbivores
B. Energy obtained by the primary carnivores
C. Energy obtained by the secondary carnivores
D. Energy of the producers not passed on to the herbivores

List-II:
I. 150
II. 750
III. 5,000
IV. 45,000

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV
A-III, B-II, C-I, D-IV
A-IV, B-II, C-I, D-III
A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I

solution.explanation: Herbivores: 10% of 50,000 = 5,000 kJ (A-III). Primary carnivores: 15% of 5,000 = 750 kJ (B-II). Secondary carnivores: 20% of 750 = 150 kJ (C-I). Energy not passed to herbivores: 50,000 − 5,000 = 45,000 kJ, lost in respiration as heat or passed to the detritus food chain (D-IV).
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap the carnivore values, or the herbivore energy with the energy not passed on.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Ecosystem', energy flow
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-III, B-II, C-I, D-IV

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Which of the following predictions about decomposition are correct according to NCERT?

(a) Identical nitrogen-rich litter decomposes faster in a warm, moist plot than in a cold plot.
(b) In waterlogged soil with anaerobic conditions, organic matter tends to build up.
(c) Leaching can carry water-soluble inorganic nutrients down into the soil horizon, where they precipitate as unavailable salts.
(d) Earthworms carry out the catabolism of detritus by secreting enzymes that convert it into simple inorganic substances.
(e) Detritus rich in lignin decomposes faster than detritus rich in water-soluble sugars.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: (a), (b), (c) and (e) only
(b), (d) and (e) only
(a), (c) and (d) only
(a), (b) and (c) only

solution.explanation: Warm, moist conditions favour decomposition (a); low temperature and anaerobiosis inhibit it, so organic matter builds up (b). In leaching, water-soluble inorganic nutrients go down into the soil horizon and get precipitated as unavailable salts (c). Earthworms are detritivores that fragment detritus; catabolism is the enzymatic degradation by bacteria and fungi (d false). Lignin- and chitin-rich detritus decomposes slowly, while nitrogen- and sugar-rich detritus decomposes quickly (e false).
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (d) or (e) contain a false statement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Ecosystem', decomposition
solution.final_answer: Option D: (a), (b) and (c) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: The sunlight available to the producers of an ecosystem is 10⁶ J. Assume that the producers convert 1 per cent of it into net primary productivity and that 10 per cent of the energy passes from each trophic level to the next. How much energy reaches the primary carnivores?

solution.explanation: NPP = 1% of 10⁶ J = 10⁴ J. Herbivores (second trophic level) get 10% of this = 10³ J. Primary carnivores (third trophic level) get 10% of that = 100 J.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10,000 J is the NPP, 1,000 J reaches the herbivores, and 10 J would be the secondary carnivores' share.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Ecosystem', energy flow; ecological pyramids
solution.final_answer: Option C: 100 J

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In a sea, the pyramid of biomass is generally inverted, while the pyramid of energy is upright.
Statement II: This shows that the 10 per cent law of energy transfer does not apply in the sea.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: the pyramid of biomass in a sea is generally inverted because the biomass of fishes far exceeds that of phytoplankton, but the pyramid of energy is always upright, because some energy is always lost as heat at each step (Statement I true). The upright energy pyramid of the sea shows that energy still decreases at each trophic level; the inverted biomass pyramid concerns standing crop at one time, not energy flow, so it gives no reason to reject the 10 per cent law (Statement II false).
steps: Energy still decreases upward → Statement II false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Ecosystem', ecological pyramids
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: India's regions of exceptionally high biodiversity are covered by three of the world's biodiversity hotspots. Which option names them?

options.text: Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, and Himalaya
Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Eastern Ghats, and Himalaya
Indo-Burma, Thar Desert, and Sundarbans
Himalaya, Eastern Ghats, and Andaman Islands

solution.explanation: NCERT: three hotspots, Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma and Himalaya, cover our country's exceptionally high biodiversity regions. Hotspots are regions with very high levels of species richness and a high degree of endemism.
solution.why_others_wrong: The Eastern Ghats, Thar Desert, Sundarbans and Andaman Islands are not among the three hotspots NCERT lists for India.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Biodiversity and Conservation', biodiversity conservation: how do we conserve biodiversity (hotspots)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, and Himalaya

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: For many taxonomic groups, species inventories are more complete in temperate than in tropical countries.
Statement II: An overwhelmingly large proportion of the species waiting to be discovered are in the tropics.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Where species remain to be discovered
solution.explanation: NCERT: there are two kinds of estimates of species numbers: those already described and an estimate of the total. For many taxonomic groups, species inventories are more complete in temperate than in tropical countries (Statement I true), and an overwhelmingly large proportion of the species waiting to be discovered are in the tropics (Statement II true).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Biodiversity and Conservation', biodiversity: how many species are there on earth
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: According to NCERT, some extreme estimates of the total number of species on earth range from:

options.text: 2 to 5 million
1.5 to 2 million
200 to 500 million
20 to 50 million

solution.explanation: NCERT: some extreme estimates range from 20 to 50 million, but a more conservative and scientifically sound estimate made by Robert May places global species diversity at about 7 million. The number of species already described is slightly more than 1.5 million (IUCN, 2004).
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.5–2 million is near the number already described; 2–5 million is below May's estimate; 200–500 million is a factor-of-ten slip.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Biodiversity and Conservation', biodiversity: how many species are there on earth
solution.final_answer: Option D: 20 to 50 million

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Nations endowed with rich biodiversity can expect to reap enormous benefits.
Reason (R): With increasing resources put into bioprospecting, the molecular, genetic and species-level diversity is being explored for products of economic importance.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Bioprospecting and the narrowly utilitarian argument
solution.explanation: NCERT (narrowly utilitarian argument): bioprospecting is exploring molecular, genetic and species-level diversity for products of economic importance. With increasing resources put into bioprospecting, nations endowed with rich biodiversity can expect to reap enormous benefits. The benefits arise because the diversity is being explored for valuable products, so R explains A.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Biodiversity and Conservation', biodiversity conservation: why should we conserve biodiversity
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: Robert May's estimate of global species diversity rests on a method described in NCERT. Biologists:

options.text: Count every species in a sample plot of tropical forest and multiply by the area of the earth
Use the slope Z of the species–area relationship for whole continents
Add up the species listed in the IUCN Red List
Make a statistical comparison of the temperate–tropical species richness of an exhaustively studied group of insects and extrapolate this ratio to other groups of animals and plants

solution.concept: How the total number of species is estimated
solution.explanation: NCERT: since an overwhelmingly large proportion of undiscovered species are in the tropics, biologists make a statistical comparison of the temperate–tropical species richness of an exhaustively studied group of insects and extrapolate this ratio to other groups of animals and plants to come up with a gross estimate of the total number of species on earth. May's conservative estimate is about 7 million.
solution.why_others_wrong: NCERT describes extrapolation of a temperate–tropical ratio, not plot counts scaled to the earth, the species–area slope or Red List totals.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Biodiversity and Conservation', biodiversity: how many species are there on earth
solution.final_answer: Option D: Make a statistical comparison of the temperate–tropical species richness of an exhaustively studied group of insects and extrapolate this ratio to other groups of animals and plants

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
A large forest is broken up by roads and farms into small, isolated fragments. According to NCERT, which of the following consequences are expected?

(a) Mammals and birds requiring large territories are badly affected.
(b) Certain animals with migratory habits are badly affected.
(c) Populations of such animals decline.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: For islands within a region, the species–area relationship is log S = log C + Z log A, with C = 10 and Z = 0.2 (area in km²). How many species are expected on an island of 1,00,000 km²?

solution.explanation: log A = log 10⁵ = 5. log S = log 10 + 0.2 × 5 = 1 + 1 = 2, so S = 10² = 100 species. Equivalently, S = C·A^Z = 10 × (10⁵)^0.2 = 10 × 10 = 100.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20,000 multiplies Z by A instead of using logarithms; 50 halves the answer; 1,000 comes from slips such as taking Z = 0.4 (log S = 1 + 2 = 3).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Biodiversity and Conservation', patterns of biodiversity: species–area relationships
solution.final_answer: Option C: 100
